Fixes grafana/grafana#87021

The Flux query editor passes `language="sql"` to the CodeEditor, so Monaco's SQL configuration makes Ctrl+/ insert `--` instead of the Flux line comment `//`.

This registers a dedicated `influx-flux` Monaco language (line comment `//`, block comment `/* */`, plus a basic Monarch tokenizer so highlighting is preserved) and uses it in `FluxQueryEditor`. It supersedes the closed attempt in #86.

Verified locally: `tsc --noEmit`, ESLint and Prettier are clean, and the Jest suite passes (32 suites, 333 tests).

issue.title: CorDA and LoRA-GA preprocessing fail with a cache filename in the current directory
issue.body:
# CorDA and LoRA-GA preprocessing fail with a cache filename in the current directory

A bare cache filename such as `cache.pt` raises `FileNotFoundError` after preprocessing. The equivalent `./cache.pt` works. I reproduced this for CorDA's `cache_file` and `covariance_file`, and LoRA-GA's `cache_file`, using a small CPU-only model without any downloaded model weights.

```python
import tempfile
import os
import torch
from peft import LoraConfig
from peft.tuners.lora.config import CordaConfig
from peft.tuners.lora.corda import preprocess_corda

torch.manual_seed(42)
model = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(4, 4))
data = torch.rand(32, 4)
config = LoraConfig(
    r=2, target_modules=["0"], init_lora_weights="corda",
    corda_config=CordaConfig(corda_method="ipm", cache_file="cache.pt"),
)
previous = os.getcwd()
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    try:
        os.chdir(directory)
        preprocess_corda(model, config, run_model=lambda: model(data))
    finally:
        os.chdir(previous)
```

Actual: `FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: ''` from `os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(cache_file), exist_ok=True)`.

Expected: save the cache in the current directory. Replacing `cache.pt` with `./cache.pt` or `nested/cache.pt` succeeds.

| Path | CorDA eigens cache | CorDA covariance cache | LoRA-GA gradient cache |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cache.pt` | FileNotFoundError | FileNotFoundError | FileNotFoundError |
| `./cache.pt` | passes | passes | passes |
| `nested/cache.pt` | passes | passes | passes |

I checked other preprocessing methods too: Astra already guards against an empty parent directory at its two cache-writing sites. I propose applying the same guard to all three affected sites and adding parametrized CPU regressions in `tests/test_initialization.py` for bare, explicitly relative and nested paths, including loading the saved caches.

I intend to contribute the fix if maintainers approve this scope. Could this be considered for `/peft-triage approved`? No implementation PR has been opened.

Environment: unchanged main `278ca0aea4dcb9ff35b15b94294338a38b9165ff`, PEFT 0.21.3.dev0, PyTorch 2.15.0, Transformers 5.22.2, Python 3.13.5, macOS CPU. This is a local reproduction, not a production incident. AI assistance was used for investigation and drafting; human review is pending.

comment.body: Hi, I'd like to work on this. The fix is to only call os.makedirs when the cache path actually has a directory part, in preprocess_corda, calib_cov_distribution and preprocess_loraga, with regression tests for bare filenames. Could this get a /peft-triage review?

issue.title: fix: use shared retry defaults for Interactions backoff

labels.name: repo-0a93f9d4
labels.description: Code changes between 40-100 lines

issue.body:
Fixes #3317

`_translate_retry_config` in `google/genai/_gaos/google_genai.py` defaulted the Interactions backoff to local constants (500ms initial, 8000ms max) and left jitter unset, while the rest of the SDK uses the documented `HttpRetryOptions` defaults from `_api_client` (1.0s initial, 60.0s max, 1.0 jitter). The same unset `HttpRetryOptions` therefore produced two different retry schedules in one client.

This change takes all three defaults from `_api_client` (`_RETRY_INITIAL_DELAY`, `_RETRY_MAX_DELAY`, `_RETRY_JITTER`), the same way `attempts` already falls back to `_api_client._RETRY_ATTEMPTS`. The local `_DEFAULT_INITIAL_INTERVAL_MS` / `_DEFAULT_MAX_INTERVAL_MS` constants are removed; explicit per-field options still override.

Tests: two new cases in `google/genai/tests/interactions/test_retry_options.py` assert that unset delay options produce the shared defaults (1000ms / 60000ms / 1000ms) and that explicit values still override. The full file passes locally (13 tests).

First public release. Scan code and dataset files for unsafe pickle deserialization — including the Hugging Face `datasets` pandas builder RCE, **CVE-2026-57845** (CVSS 8.8, affects datasets ≤ 5.1.0, no patched upstream release yet). issue.title: fix: AppProject destination deny (!name / !server) vetoes when it positively matches the cluster
issue.body:
Fixes #30588

Related to #21264 (a different mechanism: deny entries passively granting access to unmatched clusters).

What does this PR do / why do we need it:
In AppProject.isDestinationMatched, the allow case (matched := (dstServerMatched || dstNameMatched) && dstNamespaceMatched) is evaluated before the deny case, and the deny case only fires when neither identifier matched. A destination entry that combines a deny pattern on one identifier with an allow pattern on the other — e.g. {name: "!bad-cluster", server: "https://api.example.com"} — therefore permits the very cluster the deny names. This adds a positive-deny check: if the namespace matches and either identifier is a deny pattern whose body positively matches the cluster's name or server, the entry is rejected immediately.

Which issue is this PR related to: #30588

Types of changes: Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)

How has this been tested: new unit test TestAppProject_IsDestinationPermitted_DenyNameOrServer covers the name-deny and server-deny combinations, a deny-for-a-different-cluster control, and the name-only deny control. Existing TestAppProject_IsDestinationPermitted, TestAppProject_IsDestinationPermitted_PermitOnlyProjectScopedClusters and project validation tests still pass.

Checklist: I have added unit tests; existing tests pass; the change only affects destination entries where a deny pattern positively matches the cluster.

In applicationset/generators/list.go, both branches that convert list-element values to strings returned fmt.Errorf("error parsing value as string %w", err), where err is the error from the successful json.Unmarshal immediately above it — always nil at that point. issue.title: Stop requirement specifier tokens from swallowing commas after === versions
issue.body:
Fixes #1500 (and relates to #1000).

## Problem

`Requirement("x===0,>= 0")` — and every variant where a `===` specifier is followed by another specifier containing a space — raised `InvalidRequirement`, although the string is valid PEP 508 and `SpecifierSet("===0,>= 0")` accepts it.

The tokenizer's `SPECIFIER` rule reuses `Specifier._specifier_regex_str`, whose arbitrary-equality branch matches `[^\s;)]+`. Inside a requirement string that class consumes the separating comma and the next operator, so the token becomes `===0,>=` and the parse derails. The no-space form only worked because the swallowed token was later re-split by accident.

## Fix

Tokenizer-local, deliberately: `Specifier("===a,b")` allowing a comma is intentional at the API level (see `test_arbitrary_literal_with_comma_none` in tests/test_ranges.py), so the shared pattern is untouched. In `_tokenizer.py` the `SPECIFIER` rule now derives from the shared pattern with the comma added to the arbitrary-version exclusion set — in a requirement string, a comma is the specifier separator (PEP 508's version production cannot contain one).

One existing test needed an updated expectation: `test_error_when_specifier_set_rejects_parsed_specifier` pinned the old mechanism's error message for `demo===x,y`. The input is still rejected with `InvalidRequirement`; the parser itself now reports it at the right position ("Expected comma (within version specifier)...") instead of a downstream `SpecifierSet` rejection of a piece of a swallowed token.

## Tests

New parametrized regression test covers `===x,>= 1`, `===x, >=1`, `===x,!= 1.0`, and the parenthesised form. Full test suite passes (63,469 tests).

Found with property-based testing over requirement strings.

What does this PR do / why do we need it:

In `applicationset/generators/list.go`, both branches that convert list-element values to strings returned `fmt.Errorf("error parsing value as string %w", err)`, where `err` is the error from the successful `json.Unmarshal` immediately above it — always nil at that point. Go renders a nil `%w` operand as `%!w(<nil>)`, so a List generator element with a non-string value (e.g. `{"a": 1}` or `{"values": {"x": 2}}`) in legacy (non-GoTemplate) mode failed with the corrupted message "error parsing value as string %!w(<nil>)", which also loses the offending key. Both sites now return an error naming the key, e.g. `error parsing value "a" as string`.

Fixes #30850

Testing:

Added `TestGenerateListParamsNonStringValueError` covering non-string scalar, boolean, and values-map entries in both branches; the new tests fail on the unpatched code and pass with this change, and the existing `TestGenerateListParams` suite passes (`go test ./applicationset/generators/ -run TestGenerateListParams`).

issue.title: fix: anchor isValidAction patterns so prefixed or embedded verbs are rejected
issue.body:
What does this PR do / why do we need it:
In pkg/apis/application/v1alpha1/types.go, isValidAction matches the patterns "action/.*", "update/.*", "delete/.*" with regexp.MatchString, which is unanchored, so the verb may appear anywhere in the string. Actions that merely contain a valid verb therefore validated: "xupdate/y", "pre-delete/x", and "foo/action/bar" all returned true. isValidAction backs validatePolicy for AppProject role policies, so the documented grammar (exact verbs, "*", or verb/... forms) was not enforced. This change anchors the three patterns with ^. All legitimate forms in the existing test suite start with the verb, so no valid policy is affected. (Deliberately unchanged: "delete/../../etc" still validates, because it genuinely starts with "delete/" and the grammar allows an arbitrary suffix.)

Fixes #30852

TestIsValidAction gains three regression cases (NoMatchPrefixedUpdate, NoMatchPrefixedDelete, NoMatchEmbeddedAction). labels.name: user-244ae7c7/repo-234e274a
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: user-7ddb8199/repo-67cd5a00

labels.name: repo-4f6b08a3
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

issue.body:
### What happened?

`metav1.ParseToLabelSelector("tier=db,tier=web")` returns `MatchLabels{tier: web}` with no error. Converted back via `LabelSelectorAsSelector`, that selector matches `{tier: web}`.

`labels.Parse("tier=db,tier=web")` keeps both requirements, so the selector is a contradiction and matches nothing.

The conversion therefore silently widens what the selector selects for. Reversing the input order (`tier=web,tier=db`) keeps `tier=db` instead — the survivor is whichever equality comes last.

Why: `ParseToLabelSelector` (pkg/apis/meta/v1/helpers.go in apimachinery) routes Equals/DoubleEquals requirements into the `MatchLabels` map with a plain assignment, so a second conflicting equality for the same key overwrites the first. The function already returns errors for other unrepresentable inputs ("equals operator must have exactly one value"), and its doc comment says it "should be kept in sync with the parser in pkg/labels/selector.go" — it just never checks for a conflicting duplicate.

Verified non-issues: duplicate equalities with the same value, and equality combined with `in`/`notin`/exists requirements on the same key, all convert faithfully. Only conflicting Equals/DoubleEquals pairs collide.

Verified on apimachinery v0.37.2 and on the master snapshot module version v0.36.0-alpha.2.0.20261031004447-b26d01364f13. Found via property-based differential testing against `labels.Parse`.

/kind bug
/sig api-machinery

### What did you expect to happen?

Either reject a conflicting duplicate equality with an error (matching how the function already treats unrepresentable input), or preserve the semantics losslessly — e.g. route the subsequent equality for an already-mapped key into `MatchExpressions` as an `In` requirement.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Call `metav1.ParseToLabelSelector("tier=db,tier=web")`. It returns `MatchLabels{tier: web}` with no error, instead of an error or a contradictory selector. `labels.Parse("tier=db,tier=web")` matches nothing, as expected for a contradiction.

discussion.title: Potential issue: len(Headers) counts duplicate entries, disagreeing with keys()/iteration
discussion.body:
Found while property-based testing the models.

    h = httpx.Headers([("a", "1"), ("a", "2")])
    len(h)          # 2
    list(h)         # ["a"]
    list(h.keys())  # ["a"]
    dict(h)         # {"a": "1, 2"}

Headers presents a Mapping interface, and its keys()/__iter__ deduplicate — but __len__ returns len(self._list), the raw entry count, so len() disagrees with the number of keys the mapping reports. For a plain dict those always agree, and code doing len(headers) to count distinct header names gets a surprising answer when duplicates are present (which is normal for real HTTP traffic, e.g. multiple Set-Cookie... in a Headers instance built from a raw list).

Is the entry-count semantics deliberate (multidict-style) or an oversight? If it should count distinct keys, the fix is one line — len of the keys view — and I can prepare it on a fork branch. Raising it here first since it is a visible behaviour change either way, and PR creation on this repo is limited to collaborators.

discussion.title: Potential issue: a leading ":" in a URL string is silently eaten, breaking round-tripping
discussion.body:
Found while property-based testing URL parse/print round-trips.

    u = httpx.URL(":http://e/")
    str(u)                      # "http://e/"
    u.is_absolute_url           # False — parsed as a relative URL
    httpx.URL(str(u)) == u      # False — the same string re-parses as absolute, host "e"

    httpx.URL(":foo")           # accepted, colon silently dropped -> path "foo"

The URL regex's scheme group can match empty, so a leading ':' is consumed as a scheme delimiter with an empty scheme. That also bypasses validate_path's own rule — "Relative URLs cannot have a path starting with ':'" — which is enforced for component-wise construction but not for string parsing.

One wrinkle: httpx.URL("://example.com") is pinned by an existing test (test_url_no_scheme) as a deliberately supported scheme-less authority form, so a fix has to reject ":foo" / ":http://..." while keeping "://example.com" working.

The fix is ready on a fork branch: https://github.com/Sun-Wukhan/httpx/tree/fix/url-leading-colon (the full tests/models suite passes with it). Raising it here first since PR creation on this repo is limited to collaborators. Happy either way — mainly wanted to check this isn't intentional leniency.

discussion.title: Potential issue: dot-segment removal drops the trailing slash (RFC 3986 section 5.2.4), so "http://e.org/a/.." != "http://e.org/"
discussion.body:
Found while property-based testing URL normalization.

`httpx._urlparse.normalize_path` claims to implement RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, but a trailing "." or ".." segment loses its trailing slash:

    normalize_path("/..")       == ""     # RFC: "/"
    normalize_path("/a/..")     == ""     # RFC: "/"
    normalize_path("/a/.")      == "/a"   # RFC: "/a/"
    normalize_path("/a/b/..")  == "/a"   # RFC: "/a/"

User-visible consequence:

    httpx.URL("http://e.org/a/..") == httpx.URL("http://e.org/")   # False, expected True

Browsers (WHATWG) agree with the RFC here. The existing tests pin mid-path cases ("/abc/def/../ghi/./jkl" -> "/abc/ghi/jkl") but nothing with a trailing dot segment. Note the docstring example itself would change under a strict reading: normalize_path("/path/./to/somewhere/..") is currently documented as "/path/to", where the RFC algorithm gives "/path/to/" — so I wanted to check whether the current behaviour is a deliberate simplification before sending a PR.

The fix is ready on a fork branch: https://github.com/Sun-Wukhan/httpx/tree/fix/url-normalize-path-rfc (the full tests/models suite passes with it). Raising it here first since PR creation on this repo is limited to collaborators; happy for a maintainer to open the PR from the branch.

discussion.title: Potential issue: URL.host decodes IDNA only when the first label is punycode, and leaks idna exceptions
discussion.body:
Raising this here per the contributing guide, as PR creation on this repo is limited to collaborators. Found with property-based testing (per-label IDNA round-trip properties over generated hosts).

URL.host promises "IDNA hosts decoded into unicode", but the decoding only happens when the first label of the host is punycode, because the whole host string is checked with startswith("xn--"):

    >>> import httpx
    >>> httpx.URL("http://xn--fiqs8s.icom.museum/").host
    '中国.icom.museum'
    >>> httpx.URL("http://www.xn--fiqs8s.icom.museum/").host
    'www.xn--fiqs8s.icom.museum'  # expected 'www.中国.icom.museum'

The existing IDNA tests only ever place the internationalized label first, so this was not covered. The property is consumed internally by URLPattern matching and redirect handling, so an undecoded host can also affect proxy/redirect decisions.

The same accessor has a second defect: for a label that looks like punycode but does not decode, it leaks the idna package's exception types out of a property access:

    >>> httpx.URL("http://xn--a.com/").host
    idna.core.InvalidCodepoint: Codepoint U+007C ... (not httpx.InvalidURL, not a value)

The fix decodes each xn-- label individually, and leaves a label that fails to decode in its raw form instead of raising. It is ready, with regression tests for both cases, on a fork branch: https://github.com/Sun-Wukhan/httpx/tree/fix/url-host-idna-labels (the full tests/models suite passes with it). Happy for a maintainer to open the PR from it, or to open one myself if the restriction is lifted for it.

discussion.title: Potential issue: default-port normalization depends on scheme case ("HTTP://example.org:80/" keeps its port)
discussion.body:
Raising this here per the contributing guide, as PR creation on this repo is limited to collaborators. Found with property-based testing (round-trip and normalization invariants over generated URLs).

Default-port normalization currently depends on the case of the scheme, because urlparse() passes the raw scheme to normalize_port() instead of the lowercased one:

    >>> import httpx
    >>> httpx.URL("HTTP://example.org:80/") == httpx.URL("http://example.org/")
    False
    >>> httpx.URL("HTTP://example.org:80/")
    URL("http://example.org:80/")  # port 80 kept, and re-parsing this string drops it

The string form of the first URL is not even a fixpoint: str(u) re-parses to a different URL, and copy_with() silently drops the port. The URL class docstring presents an uppercase scheme ("HTTPS://...") as parsing into normalized components, and states that the scheme "is normalized to always be lowercased" — the port lookup is the one place that still uses the un-normalized form.

Schemes are case-insensitive and are normalized to lowercase everywhere else in the parser, so the port lookup should use the normalized scheme too.

I have the one-line fix plus a regression test ready on a fork branch: https://github.com/Sun-Wukhan/httpx/tree/fix/url-scheme-case-port (the full tests/models suite passes with it). Happy for a maintainer to open the PR from it, or to open one myself if the restriction is lifted for it.

issue.title: Requirement() rejects valid PEP 508 strings when a === specifier is followed by another specifier containing a space
issue.body:
Found with property-based testing over requirement strings.

These are valid per PEP 508 (whitespace is insignificant, and the version production cannot contain a comma), and `SpecifierSet` accepts the same specifier list directly — but `Requirement` rejects all of them:

>>> from packaging.requirements import Requirement
>>> Requirement("x===0,>= 0")
InvalidRequirement: Expected comma (within version specifier), semicolon (after version specifier) or end
>>> Requirement("x===0, >=0")
InvalidRequirement: (same)
>>> Requirement("x===0,!= 1.0")
InvalidRequirement: (same)
>>> Requirement("x (===0,>= 0)")
InvalidRequirement: Expected matching RIGHT_PARENTHESIS ...
>>> from packaging.specifiers import SpecifierSet
>>> SpecifierSet("===0,>= 0")
<SpecifierSet('===0,>=0')>

The no-space form "x===0,>=0" parses, but only by accident: the tokenizer's SPECIFIER rule reuses Specifier._specifier_regex_str, whose arbitrary-equality branch matches [^\s;)]+ — it consumes the comma and the next operator (the token becomes "===0,>="), and _parse_version_many then hands the pieces to be re-split. As soon as the following specifier contains a space, tokenization stops mid-operator and the parse derails, with the error pointing at the wrong place.

This reproduces on packaging 25.0 and 26.3, so it is long-standing rather than a 26.x regression. It affects anything parsing Requires-Dist metadata or requirements files where a === pin is combined with a spaced second specifier.

Note the deliberate design constraint on the other side: Specifier("===a,b") at the API level intentionally allows commas in arbitrary versions (see tests/test_ranges.py::TestToSpecifierSet::test_arbitrary_literal_with_comma_none). So the fix belongs in the tokenizer, not in the shared Specifier pattern: in a requirement string the comma is the specifier separator. Related to #1000, which covers the Specifier/SpecifierSet divergence for the same character class.

I have a fix with regression tests ready and will open a PR.

issue.title: Version.from_parts() / __replace__ validators accept bool, manufacturing unparseable versions
issue.body:
Found with property-based testing (round-trip invariant: str(Version.from_parts(...)) must re-parse).

>>> from packaging.version import Version
>>> v = Version.from_parts(epoch=True, release=(1,))
>>> str(v)
'True!1'
>>> Version(str(v))
InvalidVersion: Invalid version: 'True!1'

>>> str(Version.from_parts(release=(True, 2)))
'True.2'   # yet it compares and hashes equal to Version('1.2')

The _validate_epoch/_validate_release/_validate_pre/_validate_post/_validate_dev helpers in version.py check isinstance(x, int), which bool passes as a subclass; every other wrong type raises InvalidVersion. Reachability is programmatic only (the 26.x from_parts/__replace__ API exists to be fed transformed version data), so severity is low — but a validator that manufactures values its own string form cannot represent seems clearly unintended.

Fix: exclude bool in those validators (one shared check). I have it ready with tests and will open a PR.

issue.title: CORSMiddleware rejects empty elements in Access-Control-Request-Headers
issue.body:
# CORSMiddleware rejects empty elements in Access-Control-Request-Headers

## Description

`CORSMiddleware` may reject a preflight request when the `Access-Control-Request-Headers` field contains empty list elements, even when every non-empty header name is explicitly allowed.

For example, with:

```python
allow_headers=["x-token", "authorization"]
```

the following request header results in a `400 Disallowed CORS headers` response:

```http
Access-Control-Request-Headers: x-token, authorization
```

The same occurs with an empty element between values:

```http
Access-Control-Request-Headers: x-token, , authorization
```

## Expected behavior

RFC 9110 Section 5.6.1.2 specifies that recipients parsing comma-separated lists must ignore a reasonable number of empty list elements.

Therefore, empty elements should not cause an otherwise valid preflight request to be rejected, provided all non-empty header names are permitted by the configured CORS policy.

## Actual behavior

In `starlette/middleware/cors.py`, `CORSMiddleware.preflight_response()` splits the requested headers on commas and checks each stripped, lowercased element against `self.allow_headers`.

An empty element becomes an empty string (`""`), which is not in the configured allowlist. Consequently, the middleware adds `"headers"` to the failures list and returns HTTP 400.

## Reproduction

```python
from starlette.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

app = CORSMiddleware(
    app=lambda scope, receive, send: None,
    allow_origins=["https://example.com"],
    allow_methods=["GET"],
    allow_headers=["x-token", "authorization"],
)
```

Send a preflight request with:

```http
OPTIONS /
Origin: https://example.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: GET
Access-Control-Request-Headers: x-token, authorization
```

The request is rejected with HTTP 400.

## Proposed solution

Normalize and validate non-empty header elements while ignoring a reasonable number of empty list elements, consistent with RFC 9110 Section 5.6.1.2.

A regression test should cover both trailing and intermediate empty elements.

## Verification

The behavior was reproduced against the unpatched implementation. A local proposed fix was also tested, and the CORS middleware test module passed with 20 tests.

## Related discussion

https://github.com/Kludex/starlette/discussions/3785

comment.body:
I've prepared a fix for this on a branch: https://github.com/Sun-Wukhan/starlette/tree/fix/cors-empty-request-headers

It skips empty tokens in `preflight_response()` before the allow-list check (+2 lines in `starlette/middleware/cors.py`), with regression tests for trailing and intermediate empty elements, plus a guard test that a disallowed header next to an empty element still returns 400. The CORS test module passes locally (42 tests) and the new tests fail on the unpatched code.

I tried to open a PR but GitHub reports that pull request creation on this repository is limited to collaborators, so I can't submit it directly. Happy for a maintainer to pull the branch, or to open the PR if I'm given access.

issue.title: promql: duration expressions evaluate whole-millisecond literals 1ms short (`offset (1s1ms)` = 1s, but `offset 1s1ms` = 1.001s)
issue.body:
### Description

A duration written as an expression does not always evaluate to the same duration as the identical plain duration:

| Query | Evaluated offset |
|---|---|
| `m offset 1s1ms` | 1.001s |
| `m offset (1s1ms)` | **1s** |
| `m offset (1s + 1ms)` | **1s** |
| `m offset (-1s1ms)` | **-1s** |
| `m offset (2s500ms)` | 2.5s (correct — value-dependent) |

The plain forms store an exact `time.Duration`. Duration expressions are evaluated as float64 seconds (`promql/durations.go`, `calculateDuration`), and the final conversion truncates:

```go
return time.Duration(duration*1000) * time.Millisecond, nil
```

`1s1ms` becomes the float64 `1.001`, which is stored as `1.0009999999999998898...`; `1.001 * 1000 = 1000.9999999999999`, and truncation drops the whole final millisecond. Whether a given literal is affected depends on which way its float64 representation rounds, so the behaviour is inconsistent between values as well as between the plain and expression forms.

Rounding instead of truncating fixes it: duration literals are always a whole number of milliseconds, and float64 representation error is far below 0.5ms at any realistic magnitude.

### Relation to #20249

#20249 addresses duration *literals* in the parser (sub-millisecond and fractional values not surviving `String()` round trips) and explicitly leaves duration-expression evaluation as is. This issue is the evaluation-side inconsistency: an exactly whole-millisecond literal losing a whole millisecond when evaluated as an expression.

Found by property-based testing of the PromQL parser/engine (duration round-trip properties), then minimised to the table above.

issue.title: textparse: OpenMetrics parser does not unescape exemplar label values
issue.body:
### Description

The OpenMetrics parser (`model/textparse`, `OpenMetricsParser`) unescapes series label values but not exemplar label values. An exemplar whose label value contains an escaped character is returned with the escape sequences still in it, so the stored exemplar label value never matches the real value.

Reproducer exposition:

```
# TYPE esc_ex counter
esc_ex_total 3 # {trace_id="a\nb\"c\\d"} 1.5 1699999999.0
# EOF
```

Parsing this and reading the exemplar gives `trace_id` = `a\nb\"c\\d` (literal backslashes), while the same value in a series label is correctly unescaped to `a` + newline + `b"c\d`.

### Where

`OpenMetricsParser.Labels()` passes label names and values through `unreplace()` (openmetricsparse.go), but `OpenMetricsParser.Exemplar()` slices the raw input bytes directly into the label builder without unescaping.

### Expected

Exemplar label names/values are unescaped exactly like series label names/values, per the OpenMetrics spec's escaping rules for label values.

Found while property-based testing the text exposition parsers (round-trip / differential properties against the Prometheus text format parser, whose series-value unescaping was verified separately).
